one_liner: Dependency-free Rust language detector for 16 languages; about 5x faster than Google's CLD2 (C++) per sentence in Lingua's benchmark.
what_it_does: Whichlang identifies which of 16 languages (Arabic, Dutch, English, French, German, Hindi, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Mandarin, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Swedish, Turkish, Vietnamese) a UTF-8 string is written in. The whole API is one function, detect_language(&str) -> Lang, plus Lang::three_letter_code() and the LANGUAGES list. It returns no score, reliability flag, top-3 list or 'unknown' result, so it is not a drop-in for CLD2's detection summary.
how_it_is_fast: Detection is one pass of a hashed linear model: each ASCII character emits lowercased 2-, 3- and 4-gram features packed into a u32, each non-ASCII character emits a codepoint/128 feature and a script-class feature, each feature is hashed with MurmurHash2 into one of 4,096 buckets (the hashing trick), and the bucket's 16 f32 weights (one 64-byte row) are added to a 16-entry score array. A 1/sqrt(n) scale, per-language intercepts and an argmax finish the multiclass logistic regression. The model is a 65,536-float (256 KiB) constant table compiled into the binary, so there is no allocation, no model loading and no per-language table walk; CLD2 scores far more languages with larger n-gram tables (the link between model size and speed is inference).
when_to_use: Routing or tagging high volumes of text known to be in one of the 16 supported languages, for example choosing a tokenizer or stemmer per document in a search indexer (it was written for Quickwit).

Short and medium strings where throughput matters: its own Criterion benchmark reports 0.26 us for a 29-byte English sentence and 5.21 us for a long paragraph (about 106 to 112 MiB/s), and Lingua's benchmark puts it at about 2.2 us per sentence vs about 12 us for CLD2 (derived from page data).

Builds that cannot take a C++ toolchain or FFI: pure safe Rust with no runtime dependencies, so it compiles for any Rust target, including WebAssembly (inferred from the code; no target list is published).
Multi-threaded batch jobs: the function is stateless, and Lingua's rayon run scaled to 651.89 us for 2,000 sentences on 8 cores vs 4.81 ms for CLD2.
when_not_to_use: Text that may be in any language outside the 16: there is no 'unknown' outcome, so Polish, Ukrainian or Indonesian input is silently labelled as the nearest supported language (issues #12 'support all whatlang languages' and #16 'return Option<Lang>' are open).
When you need a confidence score or reliability flag to reject low-quality guesses: none exists (issue #24, open since 2025-08-26); CLD2 and Whatlang both return one.

Very short inputs and closely related languages: on the whatlang-accuracy-benchmark it averages 92.10% for texts of 20 characters or fewer (Spanish 76.36%, German 80.00%, Portuguese 83.87%), against 99.39% above 100 characters; the 99.5% README figure is on the author's unpublished validation set (issue #8 asks for the data).
HTML or mixed-markup input, language hints (TLD, Content-Language) or per-span language percentages: CLD2 has these and Whichlang does not.
Workloads that need retraining or new languages without Python: weights.rs is generated by the train.ipynb notebook from a dataset that is not published.

integration.platforms: any Rust target; pure safe Rust with no SIMD intrinsics, unsafe blocks or platform code
integration.thread_safety: detect_language is a pure function over constant tables and can be called from any number of threads concurrently.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — replaces CLD2's top-language call only for the 16 shared languages; no reliability flag, percentages, hints, HTML mode or unknown-language result

gotchas: Input that yields no features (an empty string) returns Lang::Eng rather than an error; version 0.1.0 panicked on an empty string (fixed in 0.1.1, October 2024), so pin 0.1.1.

Only ASCII letters are lowercased and turned into n-grams; accented Latin letters contribute only their codepoint/128 bucket and a class from a fixed list of about 40 codepoints, so languages that differ mainly in accented letters lean on that coarse signal, and the default fallback language is English.

Benchmark caveats behind the CLD2 numbers: the Criterion input is 16 distinct sentences repeated 125 times (cache-resident), CLD2 scores all of its languages while Whichlang knows 16, and the 0.28 s vs 1.70 s accuracy-reporter row also times report writing and a CLD2 adapter that converts every result by iterating up to 75 Lingua languages and allocating an ISO-code String per candidate.

The baseline binding is weak in its own right: the cld2 1.0.2 crate is marked deprecated, compiles the bundled CLD2 sources with -std=c++03 through the old gcc 0.3 build crate, and its to_c_str_or_null() returns the pointer of a CString that is dropped inside the map closure, a dangling pointer whenever a TLD or Content-Language hint is passed (not exercised by the benchmark, which uses default hints).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No other language-identification library is catalogued in string-and-text; the nearest siblings (Vaporetto, Vibrato, jieba-rs) segment text in a known language, so Whichlang is the step before them when a pipeline must first decide which tokenizer to run.
verified_claims_summary: In Lingua's Criterion benchmark (2,000 detections of 16 one-per-language sentences, iMac 3.6 GHz 8-core Core i9, compiler versions not stated), whichlang 0.1.1 took 4.47 ms vs 23.92 ms for CLD2 called through the cld2 1.0.2 crate's FFI (about 5.4x) on one thread and 651.89 us vs 4.81 ms with rayon (about 7.4x). This is a smaller 16-language model beating a larger 80-plus-language C++ detector, not like-for-like work, and the numbers were measured by Lingua's author, independent of both projects.
status_note: MIT-licensed and small, but the model has not changed since the October 2024 empty-string fix (2026 commits are CI and dependency bumps); 461 stars, about 470,000 crates.io downloads (157,751 recent) and 11 reverse dependencies including lingua as an optional benchmark dependency, while the current Quickwit Cargo.lock no longer lists it.
